Dealing with the issues of Windrush and diaspora, punctuated by bursts of catchy calypso and reggae (sound design by Mwen), Nine Night is a generously warm-hearted and moving rendering of family grief and estrangement.
Nine Night has stood the test of time and remains one of the most thoughtful explorations of Jamaican tradition and culture that has ever been written.
This revival by the Kiln’s artistic director Amit Sharma is perhaps a step towards cementing it as a classic for which productions can – and should – come about quite regularly.
Director Amit Sharma’s successful revival celebrates the pain and messiness of family funerals, with much humour and some moments that catch your breath.
A fascinating if fraught family drama.
Natasha Gordon’s Nine Night earns the title of modern classic, and Amit Sharma’s production should help to cement that legacy.
Nine Night is a generously warm-hearted and moving rendering of family grief and estrangement.
In this production, everything seems amplified: the humour is sharper and quicker, the conflicts are more intense and constantly on the verge of eruption, and the grief is even more overwhelming.
Nine Night is funny, moving, gloriously unfiltered and full of heart.

cn.t: Critics hail Nine Night's Kiln revival as a modern classic—Natasha Gordon's tragicomedy earns near-universal praise for its exquisite performances and rare balance of raucous humor and genuine emotional depth.
